subtopic_detail: Timing of glucose tolerance testing when booking body mass index is in the obese range
stem:
You are the resident at a first antenatal visit. A 33-year-old woman attends at 11 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her height is 1.62 m and her weight is 98 kg.

Her first child was born at term weighing 4350 g after a normal vaginal delivery 4 years ago. She was not tested for gestational diabetes in that pregnancy. She has no personal history of diabetes and her mother developed type 2 diabetes at 56.

She takes no regular medicines. Blood pressure today is 124/78 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein and no glucose. Booking bloods include a random glucose of 5.8 mmol/L and a glycated haemoglobin of 39 mmol/mol (<42). She asks when she will be tested for diabetes in this pregnancy, having been told she is high risk.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Anthropometry: Height 1.62 m, weight 98 kg, body mass index 37.3 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 5.8 mmol/L, glycated haemoglobin 39 mmol/mol (<42), urinalysis no protein and no glucose
data_table.History: Previous term infant 4350 g, untested for gestational diabetes in that pregnancy; mother with type 2 diabetes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for glucose testing?

options.text: Perform an early oral glucose tolerance test now, repeated at 24 to 28 weeks if the early test is normal
options.rationale: A body mass index above 35 with a previous macrosomic infant places her in the group for whom early testing is recommended so that unrecognised pre-existing hyperglycaemia is not missed through the first trimester. A normal early result does not exclude gestational diabetes developing with rising insulin resistance, so the routine test at 24 to 28 weeks is still required. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Perform an oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks only, with no additional early testing
options.rationale: Testing only in the routine window is appropriate for women without risk factors, but it delays detection of hyperglycaemia already present in the first trimester in a high risk woman. It would be correct for a woman with a normal body mass index and no previous macrosomia or family history. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Rely on the glycated haemoglobin result now, repeated at 24 to 28 weeks if this early value is normal
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin falls in pregnancy because red cell turnover accelerates, so it lacks sensitivity for gestational diabetes and is not a diagnostic test in this setting. It is useful for detecting overt pre-existing diabetes at booking when clearly elevated, not for excluding milder hyperglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange fasting capillary glucose monitoring at home now, with an oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
options.rationale: Home monitoring is a tool for managing diagnosed gestational diabetes rather than for making the diagnosis, and capillary meters lack the accuracy required for diagnostic thresholds. It becomes appropriate once a diagnosis has been established on a laboratory test. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Perform an early oral glucose tolerance test now, with no further testing required if the early test is normal
options.rationale: Insulin resistance rises substantially through the second trimester under the influence of placental hormones, so a normal early result cannot substitute for the routine test. Omitting the later test would be reasonable only if the early test had already established the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Australian practice tests for hyperglycaemia in pregnancy with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks for everyone, and adds an early test for women whose risk profile makes previously unrecognised diabetes or very early gestational diabetes likely. Risk factors that trigger early testing include a body mass index above 30, previous gestational diabetes, previous macrosomia, a first-degree relative with diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and certain ethnic backgrounds with high population prevalence. The most commonly misunderstood point is that a normal early test does not end the matter, because placental lactogen, progesterone and cortisol drive insulin resistance upward as pregnancy advances, and a woman who passes at 12 weeks may fail at 26. Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in pregnancy because accelerated erythrocyte turnover lowers it independently of glycaemia. Detecting and treating hyperglycaemia reduces macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and pre-eclampsia, which is why the testing schedule is worth getting right.
key_points: Everyone is offered a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
Early testing is added for body mass index above 30, previous macrosomia, previous gestational diabetes or a first-degree relative with diabetes
A normal early test must still be followed by the routine 24 to 28 week test
Glycated haemoglobin is lowered by accelerated red cell turnover and is not diagnostic in pregnancy
Capillary home monitoring manages established disease and does not diagnose it
explanation.pearls: Australian diagnostic thresholds on the 75 g test in pregnancy are fasting 5.1 mmol/L or above, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or above, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or above, and a single value reaching any one of them makes the diagnosis.

sources.label: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy
RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

subtopic_detail: Adolescent with cyclical pelvic pain, no menses and normal secondary sexual characteristics
stem:
You are the resident in a gynaecology clinic. A 14-year-old girl attends with her mother because she has never had a period, and for the past 8 months has had lower abdominal pain that comes for about 4 days roughly every month and then settles completely.

She has recently been getting up twice a night to pass small volumes of urine. She is otherwise well, plays netball and is doing well at school. She takes no medicines.

On examination her height is on the 60th centile and her weight on the 55th. Breast development is Tanner stage 5 and pubic hair is Tanner stage 5. The abdomen is soft with a smooth suprapubic mass palpable 4 cm above the symphysis pubis, which is not tender today. External genital inspection shows a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus that protrudes on Valsalva. Serum follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and prolactin are within normal limits, and a urinary pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Examination: Height 60th centile, weight 55th centile, breast Tanner stage 5, pubic hair Tanner stage 5, smooth non-tender suprapubic mass 4 cm above the symphysis, bluish bulging membrane at the introitus protruding on Valsalva
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and prolactin within normal limits; urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a karyotype and serum testosterone before any further examination or intervention is arranged
options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen measurement investigate a disorder of sex development, which typically presents with absent or discordant pubic hair and no cyclical pain from retained menstrual blood. They would be appropriate for absent uterus on imaging with a raised testosterone and absent pubic hair. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological surgeon for surgical incision and drainage of the obstructed outflow tract
options.rationale: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain, a palpable pelvic mass and a bulging bluish membrane indicate an obstructed but otherwise normal genital tract, and the treatment is surgical relief of the obstruction. Normal gonadotrophins confirm an intact hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis, so the problem is mechanical rather than endocrine. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress menstruation and review the symptoms in 3 months
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression relieves the pain by stopping endometrial shedding but leaves an obstructed tract with accumulated blood and risks ongoing retrograde flow and endometriosis. It would be reasonable for primary dysmenorrhoea with an unobstructed tract and normal menses. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents

options.text: Reassure that menarche can be delayed to 16 years and arrange gynaecology review in a further 12 months
options.rationale: Waiting is reasonable for absent menses with no other findings, but cyclical pain with a palpable mass indicates accumulating blood that will continue to distend the tract and compress the bladder. Observation would be correct for primary amenorrhoea at 14 with normal examination and no cyclical symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before deciding whether any intervention is required
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for complex or higher obstructions and duplicated systems, but the level of obstruction is already visible at the introitus here and imaging would delay treatment. It would be indicated if the introitus appeared normal and a higher transverse septum or duplication were suspected. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is approached by asking first whether secondary sexual characteristics are present, because their presence establishes that oestrogen production and therefore the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis are intact. When puberty has proceeded normally but menses have never appeared, the problem lies in the uterus or the outflow tract, and cyclical pain is the clue that a functioning endometrium is shedding into an obstructed space. Accumulating blood distends the vagina and then the uterus, producing a palpable mass and often urinary frequency or retention from bladder compression, which is a commonly missed presenting complaint. The differential includes an imperforate hymen, a transverse vaginal septum and cervical agenesis, and they differ substantially in surgical complexity, which is why the examination finding of a bulging membrane at the introitus matters. Prompt relief prevents further retrograde menstruation, which is associated with later endometriosis.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with primary amenorrhoea point to a uterine or outflow tract cause
Cyclical pain indicates functioning endometrium shedding into an obstructed space
Urinary frequency or retention arises from bladder compression by the distended vagina
Normal gonadotrophins exclude hypogonadism and confirm the problem is mechanical
Relieving obstruction limits retrograde menstruation and the associated endometriosis risk
explanation.pearls: A bluish bulging membrane that protrudes on Valsalva localises the obstruction to the hymen, which is a straightforward repair, whereas a normal introitus with the same cyclical picture suggests a transverse septum or cervical agenesis needing preoperative magnetic resonance imaging.

subtopic_detail: Choosing incision angle and site when performing an episiotomy at operative vaginal birth
stem:
You are the registrar conducting an assisted vaginal birth. A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is at full dilatation at 40 weeks with the vertex at station plus 2 in the direct occipito-anterior position.

She has been pushing for 2 hours and the cardiotocograph now shows recurrent late decelerations with a baseline of 150 beats per minute and reduced variability. The consultant has confirmed that a low forceps birth is appropriate and the theatre team has been notified. She has an effective epidural in situ and has consented to an assisted birth with perineal incision if required.

The perineum is short and the head is distending it with each contraction. You decide to perform an episiotomy at crowning.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, foetal heart rate baseline 150/min
data_table.Examination: Full dilatation, vertex station plus 2, direct occipito-anterior, short perineum distending with contractions, effective epidural in situ
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph: baseline 150/min with reduced variability and recurrent late decelerations

lead_in: Which incision technique is most appropriate?

options.text: Midline incision beginning at the posterior fourchette directed vertically toward the anus at crowning
options.rationale: The midline incision heals well and is less painful but extends directly into the anal sphincter and rectum with substantially higher rates of third and fourth degree injury. It is used in some overseas settings for spontaneous birth but is not recommended in Australia, particularly at instrumental birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 25 degrees from the midline at crowning
options.rationale: An angle this shallow at crowning finishes close to the midline once the perineum retracts after birth and carries a sphincter injury risk approaching that of a midline cut. Twenty five degrees would be the measured angle of a correctly placed incision assessed after delivery, not the angle to cut at. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline at crowning
options.rationale: Mediolateral incision directs the cut away from the anal sphincter complex and is the technique that reduces obstetric anal sphincter injury at operative vaginal birth. An angle near 60 degrees from the midline at the moment of crowning is required because the distended perineum straightens the incision, so a cut made at a shallower angle ends up close to the midline. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline before traction
options.rationale: Cutting before the perineum is distended produces more bleeding over a longer interval and misjudges the final angle because the tissue has not yet stretched into its delivery position. The correct timing is at crowning when the perineum is thinned and stretched over the presenting part. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Lateral incision beginning 2 cm lateral to the fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline at crowning
options.rationale: Starting lateral to the fourchette divides the vestibular tissue and Bartholin duct region rather than the perineal body, causing bleeding and poor healing without protecting the sphincter. The incision must originate at the posterior fourchette itself. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Episiotomy has moved from routine to restricted use, and the remaining clear indication is to reduce severe perineal trauma at operative vaginal birth, particularly a first instrumental birth with a short perineum. The geometry of the incision matters more than whether one is performed at all. The perineum at crowning is stretched taut, so an incision that looks adequately angled at that moment straightens toward the midline once the tissue retracts after birth, and studies measuring post-delivery angles show that a cut made at 60 degrees ends up near the 45 degree mark associated with the lowest sphincter injury rates. Every incision should be followed by systematic examination including a digital rectal examination, because a proportion of sphincter injuries are recognised only when specifically sought. Repair technique, antibiotic cover and structured follow-up all influence long-term continence outcomes.
key_points: Mediolateral technique protects the anal sphincter complex; midline incision increases severe tears
Cut at crowning when the perineum is stretched, not before traction is applied
Incise at about 60 degrees from the midline so the healed angle sits near 45 degrees
Begin at the posterior fourchette rather than lateral to it
Perform a digital rectal examination after every operative vaginal birth to detect occult sphincter injury
explanation.pearls: A mediolateral episiotomy measured at 45 degrees or more from the midline after birth is associated with the lowest rate of obstetric anal sphincter injury, which is why the incision is made at around 60 degrees while the perineum is distended.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice for a febrile pregnant woman after high risk food exposure
stem:
You are the resident in an obstetric assessment unit. A 28-year-old woman at 27 weeks in her first pregnancy presents with 2 days of fever, muscle aches and mild diarrhoea.

She attended a work function 4 days ago and ate a soft cheese platter and a prepared rockmelon salad. She has had no urinary symptoms, no cough, no rash and no contact with anyone unwell. She has not travelled overseas.

On examination the uterus is soft and non-tender and the symphysis fundal height is 27 cm. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness and the chest is clear. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 160 beats per minute with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations. Urinalysis shows no nitrites and no leucocytes, and a midstream urine specimen has been sent. Two sets of blood cultures have been collected. White cell count is 15.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) and C-reactive protein is 68 mg/L (<5).

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 108/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C, foetal heart rate baseline 160/min
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender, symphysis fundal height 27 cm, no costovertebral angle tenderness, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph baseline 160/min with normal variability and accelerations, no decelerations. Urinalysis no nitrites or leucocytes, midstream urine sent, two sets of blood cultures collected. White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone, adding azithromycin if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: All cephalosporins lack intrinsic activity against Listeria monocytogenes, so this regimen would leave the organism untreated despite being a reasonable broad spectrum choice for other causes of sepsis. Ceftriaxone would be appropriate for pyelonephritis, where the urinalysis would typically show nitrites or leucocytes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin, adding intravenous cefazolin if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin only achieves therapeutic concentrations in urine and cannot treat a bacteraemic illness, and the urinalysis gives no evidence of urinary infection. It would be correct for asymptomatic bacteriuria or uncomplicated cystitis in the second trimester. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral doxycycline, adding intravenous ceftriaxone if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: Tetracyclines are avoided after the first trimester because they bind to developing bone and teeth, and doxycycline lacks reliable listerial activity in any case. Doxycycline would be considered for suspected rickettsial illness in a non-pregnant patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin, adding gentamicin if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: A febrile pregnant woman with a systemic illness after eating soft cheese and prepared melon must be treated empirically for Listeria monocytogenes, and benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is the agent with reliable activity against it. Gentamicin is added synergistically once infection is confirmed, particularly for invasive disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Intravenous aciclovir, adding benzylpenicillin if blood cultures confirm the organism
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy treats disseminated herpes simplex or varicella, which present with vesicular lesions or hepatitis rather than a febrile diarrhoeal illness after a food exposure. Aciclovir would be indicated for a pregnant woman with varicella pneumonitis or disseminated herpes infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Pregnant women are roughly 10 to 20 times more susceptible to invasive listeriosis than the general adult population, because cell-mediated immunity is modulated to tolerate the foetus and Listeria monocytogenes is an intracellular organism controlled by that arm of immunity. The maternal illness is often unimpressive, amounting to fever, myalgia and gastrointestinal upset that looks like a viral syndrome, while the foetal consequences include miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis. The key pharmacological fact is that cephalosporins, which dominate empirical sepsis regimens, have no activity against Listeria, so a standard ceftriaxone-based approach fails precisely when the diagnosis is missed. Blood cultures are the principal diagnostic test since stool culture is insensitive and not routinely performed. High risk foods in Australia include soft and semi-soft cheeses, pre-prepared salads and cut melon, cold cooked chicken, pate and smoked seafood, and dietary counselling is a standard part of antenatal care.
key_points: Pregnancy substantially increases susceptibility to invasive Listeria monocytogenes infection
Maternal illness is mild and non-specific while foetal loss and neonatal sepsis are the major risks
Cephalosporins have no activity against Listeria, so standard sepsis regimens can miss it
Benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is first-line, with gentamicin added for synergy in invasive disease
Blood cultures are the main diagnostic test; stool culture is insensitive
explanation.pearls: Any febrile pregnant woman treated empirically with ceftriaxone alone has no listerial cover, so add benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin whenever the history includes soft cheese, pre-prepared salad, cut melon, pate or cold cooked chicken.

subtopic_detail: Surveillance after maternal seroconversion to parvovirus B19 in the second trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in a maternal foetal medicine clinic. A 30-year-old primary school teacher at 17 weeks in her second pregnancy was exposed to several children with a facial rash at work 3 weeks ago and developed joint aches in her hands 5 days ago.

She has had no fever and no rash herself. Foetal movements are not yet felt. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated.

Booking serology 8 weeks ago showed parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin G negative and immunoglobulin M negative. Repeat serology this week shows immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive. Rubella immunoglobulin G is positive from booking and her measles status is immune. An ultrasound today shows a single foetus with growth on the 50th centile, normal anatomy, an amniotic fluid index within the normal range, no ascites, no pericardial effusion and no skin oedema. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is 0.9 multiples of the median.

data_table.Investigations: Booking parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M and G both negative; current immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive. Ultrasound today: growth 50th centile, normal anatomy, normal amniotic fluid index, no ascites, pericardial effusion or skin oedema; middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity 0.9 multiples of the median

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that the foetus is unaffected and continue routine antenatal care with a growth scan at 34 weeks
options.rationale: A single normal scan performed days after seroconversion cannot exclude anaemia that typically develops over the following 2 to 8 weeks, so discharging surveillance now risks missing hydrops at its treatable stage. Routine care would be appropriate if booking serology had shown pre-existing immunoglobulin G immunity. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction testing and karyotype within the next week
options.rationale: Invasive testing carries procedure-related loss risk and confirming viral genome in amniotic fluid does not change management, which is driven by the Doppler findings. Amniocentesis has a role where maternal serology is equivocal and foetal infection must be established to guide counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.text: Administer maternal intravenous immunoglobulin now and repeat the ultrasound scan in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Maternal immunoglobulin has no established role in preventing foetal parvovirus infection or anaemia and would delay the surveillance that actually detects deterioration. Immunoglobulin is used for chronic parvovirus infection in immunocompromised adults, which is a different clinical problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange foetal blood sampling with intrauterine transfusion at the earliest available operating list
options.rationale: Transfusion is the treatment for demonstrated severe foetal anaemia and carries significant procedural risk, so it is not undertaken while Doppler velocities remain normal. It becomes indicated when middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median or hydrops develops. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.text: Weekly ultrasound with middle cerebral artery Doppler assessment for the next 12 weeks
options.rationale: Confirmed maternal seroconversion requires serial Doppler surveillance because foetal anaemia develops silently and the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity rises before hydrops becomes visible. Surveillance is maintained for 8 to 12 weeks after infection, which is the interval within which almost all foetal complications appear. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitor cells, and in a foetus with a short red cell lifespan and rapidly expanding blood volume this can produce profound aplastic anaemia, high output cardiac failure and hydrops. Risk is greatest with infection before 20 weeks and falls substantially thereafter, which places this pregnancy in the higher risk window. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is the elegant non-invasive tool here: anaemic blood has lower viscosity and flows faster, so the velocity rises well before hydrops is visible, allowing intrauterine transfusion to be offered at a stage where survival is good. Maternal infection is frequently asymptomatic or presents only with arthralgia, and the classic slapped cheek rash is a childhood feature rather than an adult one, so exposure history and serology carry the diagnosis. Spontaneous resolution of foetal anaemia occurs in a meaningful proportion of cases, which is why surveillance rather than immediate intervention is the correct posture while velocities are normal.
key_points: Risk of foetal anaemia and hydrops is highest with maternal infection before 20 weeks
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity rises with anaemia before hydrops becomes visible
Serial weekly Doppler surveillance continues for 8 to 12 weeks after seroconversion
Intrauterine transfusion is indicated once velocity exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median or hydrops appears
Maternal infection is often asymptomatic or limited to arthralgia, with no rash in most adults
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median is the transfusion threshold for foetal anaemia from any cause, parvovirus and red cell alloimmunisation alike.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy
BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection
